Exists because the key agents spend is the workspace OWNER's (RN-058) — whoever pays the bill needs to see the bill. Groups by provider because that is the unit of the credential, and separates what went out by AGENT from what went out by a person in chat: the two come out of the same key and answer different questions. Returns no secret at all.

documents.t: A SLIDING 30-day window, not the current calendar month: that is the label the screen shows, and with a calendar month the estimate would plunge on the 1st from the page turning over, not from a change in usage. Only `actor_kind = agent` counts (RN-038). An agent that never ran does not appear in the list — the screen shows a dash for it, which is different from zero.

Server-Sent Events. `delta` frames carry the incremental text and `done` closes with the token and cost accounting. documents.t: Foundation for the rich dropdown (PHASE 26b) — today the ref selector is a plain text field. `ahead`/`behind` are relative to the repository's DEFAULT branch; `null` when the provider can't compute it (an honest degradation, not an error). It is NOT `listBranches` (which the Gitflow bootstrap uses) — it is its own operation, because enriching costs an extra call to the provider PER BRANCH.
documents.s: Lists branches with ahead/behind and the associated open PR

documents.t: A null `patch` distinguishes the case where the provider didn't deliver the text (binary, or a patch too large) from the case where the text came back empty. Collapsing the two would make the screen say a changed binary didn't change. The `truncated` field warns when the file list went past the cap.
documents.s: Returns the diff of a PR, normalized across providers

documents.t: UTF-8, cut at the byte cap with `truncated: true` when it's exceeded. A path that escapes the project folder is refused with 400 by the central check in RN-095 — never with 404, which would invite probing.

Foundation for the navigable list (PHASE 26b) — today the diff is only reachable by a known id (e.g. coming from Approvals); this route resolves how to reach the id without having to know it by heart. `truncated` warns when the list went past the per-call cap.

Search is NOT a git contract operation: it is composed over the tree and the content, and so is the only read whose cost grows with the size of the repository. Three budgets cap it — directories walked, files opened, and matches returned — and `truncated` says it stopped. `filesScanned` shows the cost it incurred.
documents.s: Searches text in the repository, with a budget

documents.t: Not recursive, by contract design: the tab navigates on demand, and requesting the whole tree of a large repository is exactly the traffic amplifier this phase forbids. `truncated` warns when the level went past the entry cap.
documents.s: Lists ONE level of the repository tree

documents.t: `null` when the project was never provisioned — the common case today, because no real orchestrator transitions this table yet (RN-243/RN-267). The returned state is what was RECORDED, never confirmed against a Docker daemon: the product has no Docker client.
documents.s: Lifecycle of the project's container (recorded state)

documents.t: While the status is `sem_decisao`, the project container does not come up and the Code tab responds 409 — that's the RN-105 gate. Seeing the state requires the same permission as seeing the project, so `viewer`.
documents.s: State of the project's container (the current image decision)

documents.t: Upsert by (user, provider). The key is encrypted via envelope encryption before touching the database, and the response carries only the PROJECTION — never the secret, not even encrypted.
documents.s: Registers or replaces a provider's API key

documents.t: No role required: a credential is about whoever called, not about a workspace or project. Covers LLM keys and git tokens in the same listing.
documents.s: Lists the current user's own credentials

documents.t: Idempotent: deleting what does not exist also responds `{ ok: true }`.

The check is an explicit action, separate from registration (ADR 0050): the api decrypts the secret, calls the provider, and returns ONLY the verdict — the key never comes back, not even in part. Responds 200 for all three outcomes, because the request was processed; `refused` is an outcome, not a protocol error. 404 when there is no credential for (user, provider) — then there is nothing to test.
documents.s: Checks the ALREADY stored credential against the provider

documents.t: Requires `maintainer`, not `developer`, because the dev agents' git actions inherit the role of WHOEVER ACTIVATED it in the IAM evaluation — activating as developer would leave agents unable to open a PR. Each module in the `module_map` gets an agent in an isolated worktree.
documents.s: Activates the execution phase and starts one dev agent per module

documents.t: The most recent `active` session that already carries `execution.activated` — the SAME criterion `activate` uses to decide whether to reactivate or create one (RN-139). `null` when no execution is in progress. Exists so the Executors tab stops inferring this session from the project's most recent one, which shifts from session to session with no clue at all in the UI.
documents.s: Returns the project's current execution session, or nothing

documents.t: The project is born with the three areas (RN-094), so the list comes back full even before there is a `module_map`. What activating execution adds are the MEMBERS of the dev area, one per module.
documents.s: The project's agent areas, with each lead's cap

documents.t: Goes through the dev area CAP (RN-083): under it, the agent starts right away, in its own worktree; above it, the response is a `proposed_action` of type `parallelize` awaiting your decision, and NOTHING starts until you decide. What the cap is set to is configurable per lead in Settings.
documents.s: Requests one more dev agent for a module

documents.t: Resets the consecutive blocked-tasks counter (RN-047) and puts the agent back to trying to claim work. It is the only way out of `idle_tripped` — there is no automatic unblock.
documents.s: Rearms a dev agent tripped by the circuit breaker

documents.t: Requires `maintainer`, same reason as the parallelism cap: this is an INDEPENDENT, additive check next to the project and session budgets (ADR 0110) — not a cascade, and not a replacement for either. The limit comes in as DOLLARS and is converted to micro-USD server-side, same convention as `BudgetsController`. `null` clears the cap.
documents.s: Sets (or clears) an area's spend cap

documents.t: Requires `maintainer`, not `developer`, for the same reason as activating execution: raising the cap is deciding how much the product can spend without asking. Applies to the NEXT requests — whatever is already awaiting your decision keeps waiting.
Resets the gate correction counter and hands the task back to the agent. It is the human escape hatch for the correction cap — there is no automatic unblock.

Declarative index of the flow gates (ADR 0054). The screen derives from here which steps exist and who judges each one, instead of repeating the list in code — which is how it used to go stale unnoticed.

Validates access with `getRepo` and produces a PLAN (dry-run) of what the bootstrap would do — missing branches, missing protections, files. NOTHING is executed on the repository: decide afterward via `plan/approve` or `plan/skip`. Re-adopting the same repository converges (regenerates the plan without duplicating a row).
documents.s: Adopts an existing repository, without creating anything

documents.t: Approval is all-or-nothing: approving loose steps would break the `dev←main, qa←dev, rc←qa` cascade. What runs is the plan RE-DERIVED at execution time — equal to or smaller than what was shown, never larger.
documents.s: Approves the WHOLE plan and runs the bootstrap

documents.t: Public because whoever arrives is the user's BROWSER coming from the provider, without an api session. It isn't unrestricted: the `state` is verified by HMAC and without a valid one the call is refused. Never responds with JSON — always redirects, because a raw error body in a browser navigation would be a terrible experience.
documents.s: Receives the OAuth return and redirects to the web app

documents.t: Doesn't redirect: returns the URL for the client to decide when to send the browser. The `state` goes signed by HMAC, and that is what prevents the callback from being forged.
documents.s: Starts OAuth with the git provider

documents.t: Returns the project's provisioned repository
Which step it is on, whether it failed and where, and how many attempts there were. The step-by-step detail comes from the `bootstrap.step_*` events of the dedicated session.
`decision: null` with a plan present is the state where NOTHING runs — waiting for approval or as-is adoption (RN-045).
documents.s: Returns the bootstrap plan and what was decided about it

documents.t: The response comes back as soon as the repository exists; the bootstrap (permanent branches, protections, templates) continues in the background and is IDEMPOTENT AND RESUMABLE. Track it via `GET /projects/:id/git/bootstrap`.
documents.s: Creates the repository and triggers the Gitflow bootstrap

documents.t: `protect_branches` fails on a private repository on the free plan, and the wizard warns about this BEFOREHAND. Without this exit the only button was 'Try again', which always fails for the same reason — and `provision_failed` makes the dashboard redirect the project back to the provisioning page, leaving it unreachable forever. Only a failure in PROTECTING can be acknowledged: it is the last step and the only one whose failure leaves a usable repository. The product's merge lock (RN-006) doesn't depend on the provider's protection and keeps applying.
documents.s: Acknowledges the branch-protection failure and moves on

documents.t: Records the decision and doesn't touch the repository. The plan stays stored as evidence of what was deliberately not applied, and the bootstrap cursor is NOT tampered with — no step ran.
documents.s: Adopts the repository AS IS, dismissing the bootstrap

documents.t: Its own path, not the `users/me/credentials` one, because the body is different (`token`, and the provider enum is `github`/`gitlab`). The token is encrypted and stored without prior verification (ADR 0050); to verify it, `POST /users/me/credentials/{provider}/test`. Reading, removal, and testing reuse the `users/me/credentials` routes — it's the same table.
documents.s: Registers a git token (encrypted, without testing)

documents.t: Runs a `select 1`. Reveals only whether the database responds; no topology or version. Public because the caller is kubelet, which carries no token.
documents.s: Readiness — the process can actually serve traffic

documents.t: Does NOT touch the database, on purpose. If it did, a slow Postgres would restart ALL replicas at once and turn degradation into a total outage. The pod is pulled from the load balancer by `/health`.
documents.s: Liveness — the process still serves requests

documents.t: The registry DESCRIBES, it does not execute: no gate becomes enforced because of it, and changing a field here changes no behavior at all. Each gate says where the proof that it passed lives (`evidencia`), because not every proof is in the event log.
A specific `version` looks up by equality; omitted, it looks up the most recent `active` version. 404 if the template (or the requested version) does not exist.
documents.s: Looks up a prompt template by name

documents.t: If a version with the SAME hash already exists for the same `name`, no new version is created — the existing one is returned (the idempotency hit does not change the HTTP status: always 201, for simplicity — the body is identical to what would have been created).
documents.s: Publishes a prompt template version, idempotent by hash

documents.t: Never fails because of one provider: each one answers for itself in the report, with the reason it was skipped and the origin of the failure when there was one. A provider that did not respond is SKIPPED, not marked unavailable.
documents.s: Syncs the model catalog across all providers

documents.t: The SAME epic → story → task tree as the Backlog tab, through the same use case (three reads per project, never N+1). It is with this that the PO sees an orphan epic and a story with no task instead of re-creating what already exists (RN-164).
documents.s: The project's backlog as a tree, for the PO to read what was already written

Brabo runs the full lifecycle of an application — from brief to deploy — with a team of AI agents working over a real git repository. Creative, PO, Architect, devs per module, Infra, QA, SecOps, Psychologist and Anamnesis. Final authority is yours, and that's not a slogan: it's a property of the architecture.

No action with external effect happens on its own. Terminal command, commit, push, PR, merge, token spend — everything is born as a proposed_action, passes through the project's policy (where deny always beats allow) and only then executes. Two cases even policy can't unlock: merge into a protected branch and changing an agent's instruction. Those are ceilings, not defaults. The agent is not trustworthy by construction, and the system assumes that. It's a language model: it can hallucinate, loop, or ask for something destructive. The limits are structural — an iteration ceiling, a ceiling on fixes per task, a budget that refuses the call, a closed catalog of what Anamnesis is allowed to profile. A prompt is not a guarantee; code is. Everything that happened is recorded and immutable. The event log is append-only, with dense numbering per session. That's what makes the Psychologist's evidence traceable, cost auditable, and backups verifiable. The team improves on its own, with you in the loop. The Psychologist analyzes sessions and proposes hypotheses anchored in real events; Anamnesis derives your proficiency profile and proposes versioned instruction patches. Every patch needs your approval, and reverting creates a new version instead of erasing history.
documents.s: What sets it apart from a code assistant

Phases 1 through 26 complete, version v3.1.0. What exists: IAM/RBAC, sessions with an immutable event log, LLM router, metering and budget, an approval pipeline with permissions.json GitProvider for Local, GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and generic under a single contract, with capability declared only when proven; idempotent Gitflow bootstrap and adoption of an existing repository with the plan as a gate Full Harness and an agent hierarchy by area — lead as external contact, private internal delegation, consolidated verdict; conversational Creative, PO, Architect and Dev Lead, devs per module in isolated worktrees, QA and SecOps as PR gates, proactive Infra, Psychologist and Anamnesis with a closed loop First-party auth (argon2id, Ed25519 access, refresh rotation with family revocation) — Keycloak is gone entirely; OpenAPI locked by type across controllers, with the reference generated Nine LLM providers over a single OpenAI-compatible base, catalog with manual curation and price frozen at metering time Non-root production images, Kustomize deploy with HPA per Oban queue, graceful shutdown, OpenTelemetry, backup with tested restore Mechanized release pipeline: version computed from the branch's function, approval-ladder, promote/tag-release and backmerge with automatic back-propagation The app: the eight design-handoff screens, a read-only Code tab (tree, file with its own syntax highlighting, search, PR diff, blame and PRs in the API), a Spend tab with two audiences, a tree-shaped timeline, per-project container decided by the Architect, and its C4 diagram in the Overview What came after Phase 15 didn't come from a roadmap — it came from using the product. Program 16–26 was born from the first real navigation of the app, and every finding from live testing sessions became a rule with file:line and a test. The whole chain was proven against a real GitHub — repository adoption, story promotion, a dev agent writing code, a PR opened, a gate judging and the verdict coming back. What doesn't exist yet is stated where it matters, and is meant to be read: the known technical debt is a section, not an omission; the real-execution findings record what remains open by decision — including the two cases where the conclusion was that the path to autonomy doesn't run through loosening policy; the per-project container lifecycle is a declared cut from Phase 25, not an oversight: until it goes live, the terminal policy in ADR 0055 keeps holding as-is.

An ADR records why something was decided, at the moment it was decided. They are immutable: no ADR is edited after being accepted. When a decision changes, a new ADR is born that supersedes the previous one — that's what happened with 0018, which records the replacement of the NoopDevAgent decided in 0011. Practical consequence: an ADR can describe a state that is no longer current. For the current state, use Business rules, Architecture and the Runbook. For the reasoning, come here. Of the 61, all are accepted except those still waiting for implementation — today 0053, 0054 and 0056, marked proposed in the file itself. 0055 was accepted once it was implemented in Phase F. No check verifies this sentence: it aged saying 48 when there were already 54, and again 58 when there were already 59, and it's the argument of ADR 0029 (gerar > verificar > lembrar) confirming itself against itself.

The contract that makes Local, GitHub and GitLab interchangeable. # decision 0001 Format of the GitProvider's normalized contract: nine operations and declared capabilities, validated by a single contract suite 0002 Error normalization: six specific classes, with no common base class — the abstraction was considered and rejected for not paying for itself yet 0003 Automatic retry only on reads, never on mutations, with Full Jitter and 4 attempts 0004 Registration of git credentials: dedicated enum in the database, united with LLM providers only in type 0005 Gitflow bootstrap in six idempotent, resumable steps; skip is success

The wrapper that makes agent behavior reproducible. # decision 0006 Deterministic context assembly: ordered layers, budget per layer, predictable truncation 0007 ToolLoop, tool catalog and ContextManager — the loop with a real LLM 0008 Conversational Creative agent (chat stops being a stateless echo) and the foundation of handoffs 0009 PO, three-level backlog and rule → story → task traceability; readiness becomes a domain validation 0010 Architect: ADRs per real PR, module_map and cross-validation

Where the system starts touching real code — and where limits are born. # decision 0011 Worktrees per dev agent, git executors and the merge lock: a protected branch is never auto-approvable 0012 Real DevAgent: ToolLoop in the worktree, budget per task, ReportDone requiring a green suite, blocking with diagnosis 0013 QA and SecOps gates with an immutable-order state machine 0014 Proposal-only InfraAgent (proposes via PR, never applies) and a live team panel over Phoenix channels 0017 Workspace initialization lock, dev agent Monitor and cap inheritance for subagent corrections 0018 NoopDevAgent stops being scaffolding and becomes a permanent execution mode 0019 Unlocking the real DevAgent: writing, terminal, ADR per module and budget per project 0020 Unlocking the gates: gitleaks on the working tree (not just the diff), verdicts validated as an artifact, tool call recovery from text 0021 Closing 4a: an infra gate that really validates, and a panel that tells the truth Acceptance criterion still open. 0020 explicitly records that the gates demo is "CLOSED, but NOT DETERMINISTIC" — it depends on the judgment of a local 7B model and doesn't serve as a regression test. 0021 has a section "Acceptance criterion status: NOT CLOSED". Both are honest on purpose; don't read them as finished.

The loop that makes the team improve. # decision 0015 Real Psychologist: hypotheses with evidence pointing to real events, and light/heavy triage by cost 0016 Anamnesis: a closed catalog of competencies, versioned instruction patches with rollback, and the cap that a patch is never auto-approvable 0022 Evidence that arrives, cost that shows up, analysis that survives a kill; termination cause as a deterministic classification 0023 A catalog that works, dedup that distinguishes who declined, and a queue that survives the round

# decision 0024 Multi-stage, non-root production images, compose.prod, CI with scan and smoke test 0025 Kustomize base+overlays (not Helm), engine HPA by Oban queue depth, local overlay 0026 Graceful shutdown with drain, session registry in :global, OpenTelemetry with per-session trace, metrics and dashboards as code 0027 Tested backup/restore, rate limiting in Postgres (no Redis), classified HTTP surface and versioned release 0028 Branch protection diverges between GitHub and GitLab — and that's why it's not the gate; the gate is the domain
# decision 0029 Continuous documentation synchronization: generate > verify > remember, responsibility map validated in CI, and a mandatory escape hatch
# decision 0030 Mechanized branch policy: rule → mechanism, logic in a testable script, backmerge gate, and the cost of reintroducing each cut

# decision 0031 Auth in the api's domain: argon2id with fixed parameters, EdDSA access token from a derived key, refresh rotation with family revocation on reuse, lockout keyed on email (not id), and the single invariant that closes off enumeration

# decision 0032 The atomic Keycloak cutover: our own issuer in the guard without touching RBAC, /internal/* outside the JWT with a shared secret, web session in an httpOnly cookie with CSRF, and a migrated user indistinguishable from an email that doesn't exist 0033 The API reference comes out of the code: response DTOs that mirror the entity by type, a table test covering the summary and the real response (the one synthesized by Swagger doesn't count), and a hash manifest instead of regenerating on --check 0034 Documentation published by stage in a Pages subdirectory: baseUrl by variable, noIndex outside of main with forceIgnoreNoIndex in local search, and the third exception to direct pushes 0035 Instrument and export kept separate (trace with a real trace_id with no collector), the cross-layer path via AsyncLocalStorage + @Traced, readable log in dev and one line of JSON in production, and the three correlation gaps that were dead 0036 Auth screens faithful to the approved mock: the design system's three fonts self-hosted (the CSP blocked the CDN and typography fell back to a system font in production), the tag version baked into the artifact, contrast calculated from the tokens instead of measured by axe, and the six deliberate divergences from the mock 0037 The CORS the engine didn't have (/health returned 200 and the browser discarded it), its own plug instead of Corsica with /internal and /metrics outside the allowlist, WEB_ORIGIN read in a single place, and strictPort because the port is part of the CORS contract

# decision 0038 Area, lead and delegation: an external handoff only addresses a lead or an area-less agent, consolidation into a single artifact without changing the gates' external contract, cascading budget with a sub-cap per delegation, typed failure origin retrofitted across the whole system that already classified failure informally 0039 actionlint pinned in the engine's Dockerfile (same pattern as gitleaks/hadolint), CI pipeline validation at GENERATION time instead of a new post-PR gate, and the documented gap of .gitlab-ci.yml having no equivalent offline static linter

# decision 0040 The dashboard card and the summary line show only USD (the prices' currency of origin, with no conversion involved) — a divergence isolated to this surface, TokenMeter default/live remain in R$+US$; per-workspace currency preference with a manual rate is recorded and deferred

# decision 0041 OpenAI-compatible base over node:http (not the SDK, to get an INACTIVITY timeout), error normalized with a mandatory code in the chunk, capabilities in two layers with agent binding refused without native tool calling, and a contract suite where the contract owns the assertions and the harness owns the dialect 0042 Catalog sync by capability, with a discovered model entering disabled and a vanished model marked instead of deleted; two independent availability axes (owner curation × remote reality); a cascade that revalidates capability when it drops a level; and price frozen in token_usage so old cost stays reproducible, with append-only auditing outside the outbox 0043 The six 9b providers (NVIDIA NIM, Together, DeepInfra, Bitdeer, Vultr, OpenRouter) enter as config over the base, each investigated from scratch against the official docs — capability declared only when proven, with two real cases of a decision reverted live during implementation; the only new hook in the base is the parseErrorFrame that only OpenRouter (the hub) needed

# decision 0044 Adoption of an existing repository with origin (created|adopted) in both tables, and the PLAN as the gate: the dry-run is the check() from ADR 0005 without run(), the plan lives in the cursor (a snapshot, not a log), and nothing is changed while the decision is null — the Phase 2 runner goes out verbatim to a collaborator and is never filtered, just not called; "divergent protection" stays at the boolean level because that's all the contract exposes (ADR 0028) 0045 Event-driven dev agent rescheduling: outbox (not an in-process call) because it survives a restart between the gate's verdict and the wake; awaiting_gate holds the worktree per AGENT (not per task) until the gate finishes; delivery via PubSub (not Registry, node-local) with the at-most-once limit consciously accepted; the circuit breaker (RN-047) lives in the engine because actor.id of backlog.task_blocked doesn't identify an agent's sequence 0046 Story promotion goes back to being the user's: proposed_ready is a boolean and not a new enum value because the enum IS the claimNext gate; promoting reuses TransitionStoryUseCase (dead code from finding #13) and gets 12b's task.became_claimable for free; validation is unified in assertPromotable BEFORE the trigger becomes configurable, otherwise the two modes would be distinct rules with the same name; DIRECTED backfill (existing project goes to auto) because that behavior was already in use; the refusal is recorded before talking to the engine — the reverse of rearm, because the event asserts something about the USER, not about the engine 0047 Closing Phase 12: validation is a SCRIPT that exits != 0, not a prose script, and evidence is extracted from the database instead of transcribed; runs local and LLM-free for two verified reasons (the fork was never named; gate judgment with a local model has not been deterministic since ADR 0020), and that's declared in the first paragraph, not the footer; the Noop entered the 12b state machine — finding #10 lived on inside the very measurement instrument —, moving it to AgentIo instead of copying it; Phase 10's harvest was written with the gaps as not measured 0048 Two findings revisited: an action's DECISION (created/approved/denied) becomes a domain event with the real actor — the outbox is transport, not memory, and events.md had documented the three since forever without them existing; status in the created payload is what distinguishes a human click from policy auto-approval, the metric Phase 10 couldn't collect. And D5: the cause wasn't the worktree being recycled, it was propose/3 discarding the status and the gate opening with no PR — QA swept the worktree, approved, and the task closed without a single line committed. With the order fixed, D5 dies as a consequence, and worktree-per-task (foreseen by ADR 0045) stops being necessary | 0049 | Model curation per workspace: models.is_active was a column for the WHOLE installation — a workspace A owner turning on a model turned it on for B too, with the spend landing in the budget of whoever didn't decide. The catalog stays global because name, price and capabilities are facts about the provider, and duplicating it per workspace would create N truths about the same model besides splitting token_usage.model_id; only the decision migrates, to workspace_models. Absence of a row IS the off state — there's no third state, and that's how RN-043 survives with no column the sync could ever run over; turning off is an UPDATE, not a DELETE, so as not to erase who decided together. The picker's route hangs off the PROJECT (the three screens that consume it already had projectId, none had workspace), and isActive leaves the Model entity: whoever needs it uses a type that only exists with a workspace in hand | | 0050 | Credential always encrypted and saved; verification becomes a separate action. ADR 0004's gate (test BEFORE persisting) looked prudent and produced the worst outcome: a write-only field + refusal = a user with no credential AND no text to fix, because the screen never re-shows what they pasted. Storing and verifying are different questions, and tying them together made the second depend on the first having an answer right now. Applies to LLM and git alike — same table, same promise, and treating them differently would give two screens with distinct rules for the same object. The verdict has THREE states because the tester is a NO-OP on ollama/anthropic/openai: with a binary they'd return ok and the screen would claim a verification nobody ran (the ADR 0041 capability rule applied here). A bad key stops being an HTTP exception and becomes a 200 result, so the two @Catch that mapped it went away — a filter that can never fire is dead rule | | 0051 | Capability facets read from the provider, and "what it's for" as workspace curation. Sync never queried the remote for modality (supportsVision: local?.supportsVision ?? false), so the column was born false and died false — the 338 models from OpenRouter's first real sync all came out with no vision, including the 181 the provider declares multimodal. Image input and output become DISTINCT axes: reading a diagram and drawing one solve different problems. The other half of the request — "best for code/documentation" — doesn't exist in any catalog, and deriving it from the model's name would be a guess dressed up as data (ADR 0041); so it's the operator's opinion and lives in workspace_models, like all curation since ADR 0049. The two axes don't mix: marking a use doesn't turn the model on (the is_active column has DEFAULT true, and the new row is born with false explicit), and the screen never writes "doesn't read images", because false there means "the provider didn't declare it". Video was left out: zero models across nine providers, a filter that would never match anything | | 0052 | The dev agent waits for approval mid-loop, instead of burning iterations. The :pipeline tool pending returned the string proposed_action <id> status pending AS THE RESULT, and the ToolLoop kept going: the agent learned nothing about the command, tried something else, and died at toolloop.limit_reached {iteration: 8, max_iterations: 8} without writing a single line — approvals granted arrived after the loop had run out and were useless. The terminal allowlist doesn't solve it because it's a list of anticipated commands and the model invents commands: with read commands allowed, the same agent got stuck on git branch -a. :awaiting_approval ALREADY existed (Phase 12e, for the pr_open at the end of the task) with all the plumbing ready — outbox event, worker, Wake.deliver, worktree retention —, so what's missing is applying it mid-loop. It does NOT wait by blocking: the ToolLoop runs inside the GenServer callback, and blocking there locks the mailbox that would bring the decision itself | | 0053 | Dev Lead as an area, and parallelism authorized by the user. Today one dev goes up per module plus an extra on a one-click accept, with no session cap at all: N modules × 2 agents, and spend rises without anyone authorizing it. 14d decides that the LEAD is the one who evaluates how many agents are worth it, and that going over two in the session becomes a proposed_action through the same pipeline as any action with external effect. The Dev Lead didn't exist and was forbidden, along with dynamic areas via module_map and the generic area apparatus — the three cuts fall together because dev area members are one per module_map module, decided by the Architect and different in each project: there's no way to hardcode them like qa and infra. agent_areas/agent_area_members come in per project, with max_parallel default 2, configurable per lead; the gates' external contract doesn't change and Phase 4's suite staying green with no modification is the acceptance criterion. Anamnesis proposes raising the cap when authorization becomes routine, and never raises it on its own — automating that would be the product raising its own spend cap | | 0054 | Gates as a declarative registry in docs/gates.yml. The flow's gates existed and had been validated by real execution, but were implicit — spread across agent prompt, pure rule, use case, test and CI —, and the Phase 10/13 lesson (metric extracted by script, never handwritten) has no way to apply to what isn't enumerable. This ADR is the top half of 0048: that one made an action's DECISION observable in the event log, this one makes the set ENUMERABLE. Each gate declares evidencia: event_log | teste | ci with the locator, because not every proof is in the log — merge-protegida is a cap in a pure rule that emits no event of its own (what guarantees it is a test) and backmerge is CI with state in .release/gate.json; downgrading them to warn would lie about the product's hardest locks. The payload filter comes along with the type because qa-verificada and secops-segura both write the SAME pr.gate_changed, and the same type comes out when a gate opens with no veredito — without the filter, opening would count as passing. The REPOSITORY gates (ADR 0030) come in too — including backmerge and leaving pr-police, approval-ladder and promotion-check out would be arbitrary, they're the same family, and aprovacoes-da-escada is the only CI gate with a human decision: what it measures is people approving. Enumerating already paid off twice before measuring anything — it found the missing judgment call on infra PRs, which the list had forgotten, and found that promotion-check is a required check with NO spec of its own | | 0055 | Path scope in the terminal policy. The terminal approval ladder was MEASURED as unworkable: 15 turns, 209,031 input tokens against 4,546 output, 14 actions and ZERO lines written for the task, because almost every turn ended up waiting on a click. Two independent defects explain the "always asks": the agent emits cd <path> && <verb> and cd is in no allow list, and a composite command requires that ALL segments match (decide.ts:201), so the seeded allow is almost never reached; and "Always allow" records the WHOLE literal command, which never matches again because matching is by token prefix — the escape hatch doesn't escape. What the user is asking for, "always, as long as it's inside the project folder", is today inexpressible: only write_file has any notion of path, terminal doesn't. Execution exposed the aggravating factor: /workspace inside the executor IS the Brabo monorepo itself, and the hello-clean dev agent went as far as proposing to read git_executor.ex and context_builder.ex — there's no project boundary, and the reach is bigger than the project. Scope resolves by REALPATH and not by string prefix (a .. would escape), it PERMITS without exempting (network and install still ask; being in the folder doesn't make curl piped to a shell safe), deny still wins first, and outside the scope is require_approval, not deny. It's policy, not isolation: as long as the monorepo is mounted in the container that executes, the boundary depends on the policy getting it right | | 0056 | The engine works on a remote repository. get_local_repo_path/1 returns unsupported_provider for anything that isn't local, and four consumers stop along with it — the dev agent's worktree, the terminal executor, the diff that QA and SecOps judge, and the project context. The root cause is the asymmetry: the api speaks GitHub over HTTP (created the repo, committed, created the branches) and the engine works on the filesystem, only knowing a local bare repo; a remote project does the conversational half and stops at the construction half. That's what blocks Phase 13b from existing as writes. The git plumbing is already generic — init + remote add + fetch + checkout doesn't care whether the origin is a path or a URL —, so what's missing is a CREDENTIAL. The engine doesn't receive the master key: it asks the api for the working remote over the /internal/* channel that already exists, at the moment it needs it. And the token NEVER enters .git/config, a decision that's a direct consequence of 0055: writing https://x-access-token:TOKEN@… into origin puts the secret in plain text INSIDE the folder where RN-075 just granted the dev agent auto-approved read access — a cat .git/config would return the token, which would travel to the LLM provider on the next turn. Scope protects against reading outward, not against a secret the product placed inside. origin keeps the clean URL and authentication is injected per invocation. The credential is the OWNER's (RN-058), local stays identical, and credential failure fails with origin infra | | 0057 | The gate agent waits for approval, the way the dev agent does. ADR 0052 did this for the dev agent; the GATE agents were left out, and nobody noticed because no execution ever reached them — Phase 13b did. In the 6th real execution, qa-automacao ran ls -la && find … | head -50, a composite command with one segment outside allow: the ToolLoop correctly suspended, and QaLeadServer classified the suspension as an unexpected outcome with failureOrigin: infra. Two things wrong at once — the task was blocked by a decision nobody made, and the origin was a lie, against 0020's rule that origin is named and never obtained by elimination. The subagent gets a third outcome, {:awaiting, …}, with the whole ctx traveling along; the Lead, which was already a GenServer per project, subscribes to Wake for the SUBAGENTS (it's the actor that proposed the action that gates task.action_settled), keeps the in-flight state and continues the area from where it stopped. rodar_ativas was an Enum.map with no way to stop mid-way, and became recursion over the remainder — that shape is what allows suspending between two delegations without losing the first. While pending, the area doesn't consolidate, doesn't emit a verdict and doesn't block the task: it waits, and the click unblocks instead of arriving late. A denial also resumes, with the reason in the result's place. It does NOT eliminate approval, and shouldn't — the gate runs commands in the dev's worktree, and swapping the wall for a hole isn't solving anything; findings X, Z and AD remain open, and what changes is the wall becoming a queue. Declared limit: a restart mid-wait loses the loop, because pending lives in the lead's memory | | 0058 | CSP locked down on the api, and project scope contained at the root. Revises item 7 of 0027, which had decided contentSecurityPolicy: false because "the api serves JSON and the CSP is the web's" — true, but not the point: the alternative to a GENERIC CSP isn't no header at all, it's a SPECIFIC CSP, and for something that only serves JSON the specific one is default-src 'none', which costs zero behavior. Two paths put the api's response outside the web's CSP reach: DIRECT navigation to a route (pasted link, redirect), rendered on the api's own origin, and frame-ancestors, which only applies to the framed document. Outside production the profile loosens only what the /docs Swagger UI needs, under the SAME condition that mounts Swagger — if it ever goes up in production, the CSP follows instead of silently blocking it. The options moved out of the main.ts literal into security-headers.ts for the same reason that already moved cors-origins.ts: at boot they weren't testable, and the proof has to be a real request, because false and a directives object are both "valid config" and only differ in the HTTP response. Along with it comes containing projectId: it arrives from the route parameter already percent-decoded by Express, so ..%2F..%2Fetc became ../../etc and escaped the root — hitting not just reading and WRITING permissions.json but also the scope that AUTHORIZES the terminal via 0055, i.e., the policy pointing at the wrong place. Validation lives where the root is derived, not in each caller, for the same reason the function exists: duplicated checking is checking that one day diverges. Also records the seven CodeQL dismissals with the reason for each — among them js/insufficient-password-hash over an OAuth state HMAC, where there's no password and a slow hash would be a mistake | | 0059 | The key that signs the git OAuth state has no default. Born from one of 0058's dismissals: dismissing js/insufficient-password-hash was right — there's no password there, the "password" is GIT_OAUTH_STATE_SECRET, a server-side HMAC key, and HMAC-SHA256 is the right primitive. What the argument didn't consider is that a server key with a known default value signs nothing, and that was the case: both read points did process.env.GIT_OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? 'dev-oauth-state-secret-change-me'. The same failure mode WEB_ORIGIN had already had closed in cors-origins.ts, and worse for two reasons — the value is PUBLIC (it's in the .env.example of an open-source repo, not a weak default, a published secret), and what it protects is the state, the only obstacle to forging the callback of a route that needs to be public: with the key known, anyone can sign {projectId, userId, provider} of their choice and make the callback write, into that payload's project, the git token obtained from the provider. The detail that decides the shape of the fix is that docker-compose.prod.yml supplied the literal as a fallback, so on the REAL error path the variable WAS defined — requiring just "not empty" wouldn't have caught anything, and that's why the example literal is rejected explicitly, along with a 16-character floor that turns the configuration table's ever-present "weak = CSRF" into an actual check. The check runs at BOOT, not on first use: an api that only failed when someone tried to connect git would stand for weeks accepting a state signed with a public key. Resolved into a single function for the RN-092 reason — there were two copies of the same literal, and diverging them would make the callback reject every legitimate state. Deliberate breakage: production with no variable set stops booting, which is the goal and not a side effect. The four sibling secrets of the same compose (AUTH_JWT_SECRET, BRABO_SERVICE_TOKEN, CREDENTIALS_MASTER_KEY, SECRET_KEY_BASE) were left declaredly out, in the backlog — closed later by the same rule, with no new ADR, in RN-114 | | 0060 | The Code tab's code-reading surface, contained and budgeted. 26a put listTree and getPullRequestDiff into the contract and installed the check that fails an operation with no consumer; this ADR is the consumer, and deciding to write it forced resolving three things no prior route had faced, because none received a FILE PATH from the client. Where the search lives: outside the contract. None of the three providers has it — GitHub and GitLab have platform-level code search with their own semantics, and LocalGitProvider is a bare repo —, so declaring it would either be a 13th operation with false capability on local (a tab that vanishes on one provider) or leaking a platform's vocabulary into the normalized contract that exists precisely to prevent that; it stays composed at the application level, over listTree + getFileContent. How much it can spend: three budgets (directories walked, files opened, matches returned) plus a short-TTL cache, because it's the only read whose cost grows with the repository's SIZE and not with the request's, and who pays is the OWNER's credential (RN-058/RN-082) — with no cap it's the same failure family as the dashboard's 3,824 req/min, with 429 turning into a blank screen. Breadth-first scan: cut off midway, it delivers the shallow files, which is where one usually looks. How the path is contained: a single function, in the RN-092 file, reusing the scope primitives from 0055 — and returning the NORMALIZED path, because returning the original would allow checking one string and sending another. The vector isn't reading the wrong file: on a remote provider the path becomes a URL segment of the API and a .. SWITCHES ENDPOINT with the owner's token in hand. CodeQL will keep flagging it, and the price is the one already accepted in the POST-PHASE 15 — duplicating the check would silence the alert and create four copies that one day diverge. The four routes are GET/role:viewer and the controller has NO write verb: reading isn't an external effect and doesn't become a proposed_action (it would flood the queue with noise), and when writing arrives it's born as one — the absence of a verb is what makes this boundary verifiable instead of an intention | | 0061 | The session's type is creation-time data, and execution stays an event. Every session was born the same, and reaching the Creative agent meant opening it first and DISCOVERING a button in the top bar afterward — that's how the user reported the problem. The risk isn't the new field: it's that the product ALREADY knew how to tell an executing session apart, by derivation, and findActiveExecutionSession looks for the active session that carries execution.activated (that's what makes reactivating land on the session where the dev agents already are, finding #11 of the first dogfooding). Recording a type creates a SECOND source, and two sources diverge — here, over where the dev agents write. Deriving everything from the log doesn't work, and the reason is temporal: the intent exists BEFORE any event, in the click that opens the session, and a creative session nobody activated has no event to derive from. The decision is that the two coexist answering different questions — kind is creation INTENT and immutable, the event is execution STATE, and findActiveExecutionSession does NOT start looking at kind —, under the rule that keeps them from fighting: execution.activated on a consultiva session is 409, never silent conversion. The lock lives in the FUNNEL (AppendSessionEventUseCase), because both the user's route and the engine's /internal/* pass through it, and locking in the use case would leave the other open; and it runs before incrementSeq, so a rejected attempt doesn't consume seq. The field is mandatory at every creation point, including the four internal ones: optional would make the other callers silently inherit the default. The column's DEFAULT is consultiva (the type that can do less) and the BACKFILL is criativa, in the opposite direction and by the argument of 0046 — every existing row predates the distinction, and some are the sessions the dev agents are working in right now. Along with it come the friendly name, which is ADDED to the hashtag and never replaces it (the hashtag is what gets pasted into a URL; a person's name isn't unique), and the session screen's exit, which had none. The accepted price: the question "does this session execute?" now has two places to check | | 0063 | Two audiences for the same spend: the owner's bill and the member's consumption. The request was a spend summary tab in the spirit of OpenRouter's activity, and the data was never the problem — token_usage has provider, model, actor, tokens and price FROZEN since 0042; what was missing was the AGGREGATIONS (there was none by model, by project within the workspace, by session or by person). The difficulty is the collision between two existing rules: by RN-058 the key the agent spends is the OWNER's, and by RN-060 that key's bill is his and only his — so "how much did I spend" is, literally, asking for a slice of someone else's bill. The two easy outs are both wrong: opening the credential report filtered revokes RN-060 through the back door (the answer would still talk about provider and key, and summing the lines reconstructs the bill), and showing nothing leaves the one person forbidden from seeing the consumption being exactly the one who is it. The decision separates the QUESTIONS: the owner's is by CREDENTIAL (provider, key, bill) and still requires owner, reused whole instead of rewritten; the member's is by ACTOR, in tokens and estimated cost, WITHOUT breaking down by provider or credential. Declared, not hidden: conversion never copies code between scope roots — the engine re-derives the worktree from the project's bare repo on demand (Engine.Actions.Workspace.ensure!/4), so committed work is safe but an UNCOMMITTED diff in the abandoned old worktree is orphaned in place, not migrated and not deleted | | 0112 | Standalone binary of @brabo/runner via bun build --compile — companion of ADR 0106, closing the ADR 0104 backlog item explicitly deferred there. node-pty resolves its own native .node addon by a path COMPUTED at runtime, which Bun can't embed statically (proven empirically: the naive build compiles clean and throws at runtime); the fix embeds every file node-pty needs via with { type: 'file' } (the only Bun mechanism that accepts a literal specifier) and re-extracts them to a REAL temp directory at startup, preserving the original relative layout so node-pty's own relative require() calls resolve unmodified. Two bugs found only by running the compiled binary: --external node-pty is required on the bun build command itself (Bun silently bundles the non-compiled fallback's await import('node-pty') otherwise, throwing a misleading error at runtime instead of failing the build), and the ADR 0106 auto-run guard needed a second branch for process.argv[1] being a virtual /$bunfs/root/... path inside a compiled binary. Five-target matrix (linux-x64/linux-arm64/darwin-x64/darwin-arm64/win32-x64), each built on its own native runner; only linux-x64 was validated by real execution in this investigation — the other four, Windows especially, are reasoned through node-pty's source, with their first real execution being the next version tag |

One file per decision, at docs/adr/NNNN-short-title.md, with sequential 4-digit numbering. No number reuse, not even when an ADR is superseded — the next one is 0113. Three sections, only those: Context (the problem or force that motivated it), Decision (what was decided), Consequences (the accepted trade-offs and what's left for later). No third-party template — no Nygard, MADR or variants. The three sections are enough. In Portuguese, like the rest of the project. An accepted ADR is not edited. One superseded by a later decision stays as it is; the new ADR references the old one and explains what changed. What gives these ADRs their value is recording what did not work: 0020 documents nine failed executions in a row, and 0027 records a justification that was revised within the same session that produced it. An omitted bad consequence is the part that's missed six months later.

Phase 2 (CLAUDE.md) calls for a normalized GitProvider interface in packages/shared covering 8 operations (createRepo, getRepo, createBranch, protectBranch, commitFiles, listBranches, openPullRequest, mergePullRequest), with types that never leak the shape of Octokit (GitHub) or the GitLab REST client (@gitbeaker), plus a capabilities object through which the domain degrades when an operation isn't supported by a provider. Before this session, apps/api already had a GitProvider — but as an abstract class used as a NestJS dependency-injection token, with a single operation (createRepository), consumed by the repository provisioning pipeline already in production (ProvisionRepositoryUseCase, GitProviderRegistry, GitInfrastructureModule). This session is scoped only to the "foundation" (types + contract suite + complete LocalGitProvider) — finishing GithubProvider/GitlabProvider for the 8 operations is left for a future session.

Two contracts deliberately coexist for now: GitProvider (unchanged, apps/api/src/application/ports/git-provider.port.ts) — remains the Nest DI token, with createRepository. Nothing in it changes this session; GithubProvider/GitlabProvider/the registry/ the provisioning use case are not touched. GitProviderContract (new, packages/shared/src/index.ts) — the normalized interface with 8 operations + capabilities, types GitRepo/GitBranch/GitPullRequest/GitCommitResult. Not wired to any DI token yet. Only LocalGitProvider implements it for now (in addition to continuing to implement the old, unchanged GitProvider). Named GitProviderContract instead of reusing the GitProvider identifier — this avoids a name collision in the file that implements both (LocalGitProvider) and matches the "contract suite" vocabulary that CLAUDE.md itself already uses to describe the tests. Every repository identification field uses externalId (not id or repoId) — the same name already used by CreateRepositoryResult/ ProvisionedRepository, to stay consistent with what's already persisted. capabilities: { protectBranch: boolean; pullRequests: boolean } — two boolean flags, introspectable at runtime (provider.capabilities.protectBranch), with no per-operation granularity beyond that (e.g. there's no "partial protectBranch"). LocalGitProvider declares both as false — a local bare repo has no platform behind it to host branch protection or pull requests. When an operation gated by a missing capability is called, the provider throws GitNotSupportedError (never a raw crash) — see 0002. Merge/PR on local: openPullRequest and mergePullRequest on LocalGitProvider throw GitNotSupportedError unconditionally — there is no simulated PR via branch+direct merge in this session. A future Gitflow bootstrap session will likely need a direct-merge operation (not a "fake PR") for providers without pullRequests — that operation is deliberately not modeled here yet, so as not to invent an API surface nobody consumes yet.

Zero regression risk in the provisioning pipeline already in production — GitProvider/GithubProvider/GitlabProvider remain exactly as they were. Explicit debt: the two contracts (GitProvider and GitProviderContract) need to converge in a future session, once GithubProvider/GitlabProvider also implement GitProviderContract — at that point it makes sense to retire GitProvider (the old one) in favor of the new one, or have one of them extend the other. The contract suite (apps/api/test/contract/git-provider.contract.ts) is already written in a reusable way — it branches on provider.capabilities.* to decide the right assertion — so it won't need to change when Github/Gitlab come in, only the harness that invokes it changes.

The "explicit debt" from the previous section has been paid: GithubProvider and GitlabProvider already fully implemented GitProviderContract since the git credentials session (with the mocked contract suite passing on all 3 providers). In this session, GitProviderRegistry.get() started returning GitProviderContract instead of the legacy GitProvider — createRepository/CreateRepositoryInput/CreateRepositoryResult were removed (confirmed by grep: ProvisionRepositoryUseCase was the only consumer). The contract also gained a 9th operation, getFileContent, needed for the bootstrap to verify "file already committed with the same content" before recommitting — see docs/adr/0005-repo-bootstrap-idempotent-steps.md.

The GitProviderContract contract suite (see 0001) needs normalized, stable errors for the 8 operations — in particular the 3 scenarios cited in the original request (repository already exists, branch not found, permission denied) plus the missing-capability case, which can never be a raw crash. The rest of the codebase already has a domain-error convention: each error is a standalone class X extends Error, with this.name set explicitly and typed context fields (never a generic code enum) — see apps/api/src/domain/git/git-provider-errors.ts (GitProviderAuthError, InvalidOauthStateError, focused on OAuth) and the session/action state-machine errors.

No common base class. Introducing an abstract GitError extends Error for the 6 new classes to converge on was considered, and rejected: no new HTTP filter is registered in this session (no endpoint exposes the 8 operations yet — that's items 4-6 of Phase 2, future work), so a common base has no immediate use, and it would deviate from the "no base" convention already established across the rest of the domain for no concrete reason right now. Six standalone classes in apps/api/src/domain/git/git-errors.ts (new file, separate from the OAuth git-provider-errors.ts): GitRepoAlreadyExistsError(repoId) GitRepoNotFoundError(repoId) GitBranchNotFoundError(repoId, ref) GitBranchAlreadyExistsError(repoId, branchName) — falls out for free from the compare-and-swap semantics of git update-ref used in createBranch; it wasn't part of the original list of 3 scenarios, but it's the natural behavior of rejecting an overwrite of an existing branch. GitPermissionDeniedError(path) GitNotSupportedError(provider, operation) Permission-denied test and containers running as root. The api's dev containers run as root (docker/api/Dockerfile, no USER). Root bypasses Unix permission checks (DAC), so a test that does chmod(dir, 0o000) and expects EACCES doesn't reproduce anything real when running as root — the test would "pass" without exercising any error-handling code, which is worse than not having the test at all. Considered (and deferred, out of proportion for this session's scope): using Node's child_process uid/gid options to deliberately drop privilege before attempting the operation — this would require assuming a specific unprivileged uid (nobody or similar) present in every environment where the suite runs, and would add an identity-override path just for the test's benefit. Decision: the suite detects process.getuid?.() === 0 and skips (it.skipIf) the permission-denied test when running as root, with an explicit comment in the code — it never pretends to have passed.

No HTTP filter (@Catch(...)) is added in this session — it's left pending for when a future session exposes the 8 operations via endpoint (items 4-6 of Phase 2). Until then, these 6 classes only circulate inside the api process (direct calls to the provider, tests). In environments where tests run as a non-root user (e.g. CI configured without root, or a future dev image with a non-root USER), the permission-denied test starts being exercised for real — no code change is needed for that to happen, just the environment.

GithubProvider and GitlabProvider make real network calls (Octokit and Gitbeaker) that fail transiently — rate-limiting (429), 5xx errors, timeouts. The 8 operations of GitProviderContract (see 0001) split into two very different natures regarding safe re-execution: Reads (getRepo, listBranches) are idempotent by nature — re-running them has no side effect. Mutations (createRepo, createBranch, protectBranch, commitFiles, openPullRequest, mergePullRequest) are not generically idempotent (e.g. resending createRepo after a timeout can collide with the very repository the first attempt created, or trigger a second commit) — deciding whether/how to re-run depends on context the retry wrapper doesn't have.

Automatic retry only on reads, never on mutations. apps/api/src/infrastructure/git/retry.ts exposes withRetry(fn, options) with "Full Jitter" (AWS's algorithm: sleep = random(0, min(maxDelay, base·2^attempt))), maxAttempts default 4, baseDelayMs 250, maxDelayMs 4000. Only getRepo/listBranches on the two remote providers go through withRetry; every mutation calls the API directly and lets the error bubble up raw on the first failure — the caller decides whether to try again. Retry criteria are per-provider, not generic, via a shouldRetry: (error) => boolean passed to each call: GitHub (isRetryableReadError in github-provider.ts): 429, or any 5xx, or 403 only when the x-ratelimit-remaining: 0 header confirms rate-limiting (isRateLimited) — GitHub overloads 403 for both permission-denied AND rate-limit, and only the header distinguishes the two; it never retries a 403 by status alone (retrying a permission denial is infinite and useless). GitLab (isRetryableReadError in gitlab-provider.ts): only GitbeakerTimeoutError and 500/503/504. Gitbeaker already retries 429/502 internally (exponential backoff without jitter, up to 10 attempts) — adding a retry here for those codes would double the total delay for no gain; the wrapper only covers what Gitbeaker doesn't handle. Known caveat, out of our control: Gitbeaker's built-in retry is per-TRANSPORT, not per-operation. @gitbeaker/rest's defaultRequestHandler (retryCodes = [429, 502], maxRetries = 10, delay 2^attempt · 0.25s, no jitter) runs for ANY HTTP request the client makes — GET, POST, PUT, without distinguishing reads from mutations — and both values (retryCodes, maxRetries) are internal module constants, with no public option on the Gitlab(...) constructor to disable or reconfigure them (confirmed by reading @gitbeaker/rest@43.8.0 — no customizable requesterFn exposed by the aggregated class used here). In practice this means a GitlabProvider mutation that responds with 429 or 502 is retried anyway, just by the lib rather than by our withRetry — the guarantee "a mutation never retries automatically" is only 100% true for GitHub (Octokit embeds no retry at all: neither @octokit/plugin-retry nor plugin-throttling are among the dependencies) and, for GitLab, is only true for the codes Gitbeaker does NOT handle (400, 403, 404, 422, 500, 503, 504) — 429/502 escape outside our control. See the test GitlabProvider — cenários de HTTP mockados > 429 numa mutação (createRepo): o Gitbeaker retenta por conta própria (gitlab-provider.contract.spec.ts), which documents this real behavior instead of pretending it doesn't exist, and the test with 500 (outside Gitbeaker's list) that proves "no retry" at both layers at once.

A GitHub mutation that fails due to rate-limiting or 5xx always rejects on the first attempt — there is no automatic write retry at this stage. If this proves to be a real UX problem (e.g. Gitflow bootstrap failing due to transient rate-limiting), the future decision is about idempotent retry per specific operation (e.g. createBranch could check whether the branch already exists before re-running), not a generic wrapper. A GitLab mutation that fails with 429/502 is retried by Gitbeaker (up to 10x, ~29s of accumulated wait in the worst case: sum of 0.25·(2^10-1) seconds) BEFORE our code even sees the error — accepted as a documented, non-hidden library limitation. Swapping libraries just because of this is disproportionate at this stage; if it becomes a real problem (e.g. a createRepo duplicated by improper re-execution on top of rate-limiting), the future decision is about replacing @gitbeaker/rest with a thin HTTP client that gives full control over retry, not about working around the behavior from the outside. withRetry has no coupling to Octokit/Gitbeaker — it's tested in isolation (retry.spec.ts) with a generic fn, and each provider only supplies its own shouldRetry. The total wait time on a read with all attempts exhausted is bounded by maxDelayMs (4s) per attempt, not by a total-time ceiling — in the worst case (4 attempts, each at the cap), the wait sums to up to ~12s before the final error bubbles up.

Item 3 of Phase 2 (see CLAUDE.md): the user's git credentials (GitHub/GitLab tokens used by GithubProvider/GitlabProvider to operate on their behalf) need to live in the same user_credentials table as the LLM API keys (Phase 1), with the same envelope encryption, and with a mandatory connection test at registration time. Two shape questions: user_credentials.provider was already an llm_provider enum (ollama/anthropic/...). A git token isn't an LLM provider — widening llm_provider would mix two domains into a single enum also used by models/token_usage (genuinely LLM-only). Reusing git_provider (used by project_git_connections) doesn't work either: it includes 'local', which makes no sense as a credential provider (there's no token for local git). An invalid/revoked token is only discovered when it's actually used — without a connection test, registration "succeeds" and the failure only surfaces at the first Gitflow bootstrap, much later and more costly to diagnose.

Dedicated enum credential_provider (migration 0007), with CredentialProviderName = LLMProviderName | GitCredentialProviderName in packages/shared — a union of the two domains only in the type used by UserCredentialRepository, without mixing the database enums. GitCredentialProviderName is Extract<GitProviderName, 'github' | 'gitlab'> — it derives from the git provider enum instead of duplicating the list, but structurally excludes 'local'. SYNCHRONOUS and MANDATORY connection test before encrypting/persisting. RegisterGitCredentialUseCase.execute (new) calls GitCredentialConnectionTester.test(provider, token) first; only if that resolves is the token encrypted (EncryptionService.encrypt) and written (UserCredentialRepository.upsert). On a failure, nothing is written — see GitCredentialConnectionTestFailedError in domain/git/git-errors.ts. The real implementation (GitCredentialConnectionTesterImpl) makes the cheapest possible call on each API to confirm the token authenticates: GET /user (Octokit users.getAuthenticated) on GitHub, GET /user (Gitbeaker Users.showCurrentUser) on GitLab — neither attempts to list repos or anything that depends on scope beyond basic authentication. PAT always via token: in Gitbeaker, never oauthToken:. GitLab validates the two differently (PRIVATE-TOKEN header vs. Authorization: Bearer) — they aren't interchangeable. oauthToken is reserved for the project-level OAuth flow (project_git_connections, Phase 2 item 4+), which this session doesn't change. Dedicated endpoint only for registration; GET/DELETE reused. POST /users/me/git-credentials (new, GitCredentialsController) is the only path in this session, because only registration needs the synchronous connection test. Listing and deletion already existed in CredentialsController (Phase 1, LLM) over the same table/repository — UserCredentialRepository was widened from LLMProviderName to CredentialProviderName (it was the loose LLMProviderName left over that broke the build, see delete() in user-credential.repository.ts) instead of duplicating list/delete for git. No @RequireRole on the new controller: it's about the authenticated user's own credential, the same pattern as the equivalent LLM endpoint. Connection failure maps to 422, not 400 or 409 (git-provider-error.filter.ts): it's neither malformed payload (400) nor a conflict with existing state (409) — it's a semantically invalid entity (a token that never authenticated), the textbook 422 case.

Registering a git credential now makes a synchronous network call to the provider's API before responding — the endpoint is slower than a "blind" registration, deliberately (see Decision). UserCredentialRepository (and its migration 0007) now serves two domains (LLM and git) through the same table/type enum — any future credential provider (git or otherwise) enters through CredentialProviderName, not a new enum. The connection test isn't retried (GitCredentialConnectionTester doesn't use withRetry, see 0003) — a transient network failure during registration requires the user to try again manually; acceptable because it's a one-off interactive action, not a background operation.

Phase 2, session 3 ("the heart"): ProvisionRepositoryUseCase, in addition to creating the repository, now runs the full Gitflow bootstrap (dev/qa/rc branches, protections per capabilities, PR template, docs/branching-policy.md) as a sequence of steps that needs to: converge to the same state no matter how many times it runs (idempotence), resume from where it stopped after a mid-run crash (progress persistence), and narrate every mutation as an auto_approved proposed_action in the session's event log — all of this with no precedent in the codebase (the first "kill the process mid-way and resume" feature in this repository). Two decisions were explicitly confirmed with the user before implementation; the rest was resolved during implementation, as integration with existing code (sessions, proposed_actions, GitProviderContract) revealed real constraints.

1. getFileContent as the GitProviderContract's 9th operation. The "file already committed with the same content" check (idempotence of commit steps) can't be done with the original 8 operations — none of them reads file content. Confirmed with the user: add getFileContent(externalId, branch, path): Promise<string | null>, implemented across the 3 providers (LocalGitProvider via git show, GithubProvider via Octokit repos.getContent, GitlabProvider via Gitbeaker RepositoryFiles.show), covered by the single contract suite. The GitHub/GitLab fake backends (msw) had to start tracking real content (previously only branch/PR metadata) — a blob→tree→commit graph for GitHub (mirrors the real API), a path→content map per branch for GitLab (the commit API sends the full state at once). 2. A dedicated session, created once and reused on every resume. proposed_actions/session_events require an existing sessionId — there's no support for an action/event "without a session". Confirmed with the user: ProvisionRepositoryUseCase creates ONE session per project on the first attempt (the same cheap mechanism as CreateSessionUseCase — just an INSERT + an outbox event, never calls the engine), stores its id in repo_bootstraps.session_id, and REUSES it on every resume — the bootstrap's history (success, failure, resume, skips) stays narrated as a continuous timeline, not fragmented across sessions. The session never transitions to active via TransitionSessionUseCase (which would call the engine through ApiToEngineClient.startSession — wrong for a session that never runs any command): the created→active transition is done directly via SessionRepository.updateStatus, guarded by assertTransition. For the same reason, the session NEVER goes to closed_abnormally on a step failure — that's a terminal state (no outgoing transitions, session-state-machine.ts) and would break reuse across future resumes; it stays active through any number of failed attempts/resumes, only closing (closing→closed, without touching the engine on either hop) once all 6 steps converge in the same run. 3. A single cursor per project, full revalidation on every run. repo_bootstraps is one row per project (not a log per step) — {project_id, session_id, step, status, attempts, last_error}. Idempotence does NOT come from skipping steps based on that cursor: EVERY run (fresh or resumed) walks through all 6 steps from the start, calling each one's check() against the real state on the provider — only when check() reports "not satisfied" does an actual mutation happen. The cursor is only a diagnostic (last step touched + result), never a gate. This single rule gives, for free: idempotence (running N times = every check() returns satisfied, zero mutations), resumption after a failure (the steps already done remain satisfied, only what's missing runs), and resumption after "killing the process mid-mutation" (the row is left with status=running; on the next run check() discovers the mutation actually already happened and skips it) — the 3 scenarios from the acceptance criteria (item 6) are the SAME mechanism, not three separate implementations. 4. No decide() in the bootstrap's path — status is born hardcoded as auto_approved. The request says "auto_approved decision for the bootstrap". Calling the real decide() (the way ProposeActionUseCase does for user/agent actions) would NOT produce that by default: decide()'s fallback when no rule in permissions.json applies is require_approval, never auto_approve. In other words, always-auto-approved bootstrap only makes sense as a structural category separate from the discretionary pipeline, not as "the typical result of decide() for a new project". Structurally safe: auto_approved is never a transition destination in action-state-machine.ts (only an initial state), so hardcoding it at creation doesn't violate the state machine. Accepted consequence: a deny in permissions.json targeting git_branch_create etc. does not block the bootstrap — it's new-project infrastructure, not a discretionary agent/user action. 5. Step EXECUTION order differs from the order listed in the request. The request lists "create dev from main" first, with commits last. That's impossible as stated: createRepo creates an empty bare repo, with no initial commit, on all 3 providers (auto_init: false — "provisioned" needs to mean the same thing everywhere), and a ref with no commits can't be the source of createBranch. The two commits on main (PR template, branching-policy.md) need to come FIRST — they are what give main its first commit. Real execution order (BOOTSTRAP_STEP_SEQUENCE/BOOTSTRAP_STEPS, kept in sync): commit_pr_template → commit_branching_policy → create_dev_branch → create_qa_branch → create_rc_branch → protect_branches. The branch cascade is dev←main, qa←dev, rc←qa (my default — the request doesn't specify the origin of qa/rc; it follows the dev→qa→rc→main promotion pipeline described in CLAUDE.md). The bootstrap_step enum in the schema (declaration order) didn't need to change — it's never compared by order, only by equality. 6. No 409 for reprovisioning an already-converged project. The previous version of ProvisionRepositoryUseCase threw a ConflictException if a repo already existed for the project. Keeping that guard would have broken idempotence: "running the use case N times converges without error" (item 2 of the request) is incompatible with "the 2nd call throws 409". Resolved: no conflict guard in that sense — an already-converged project just makes all 6 check()s report satisfied (a pure skip), never an error. 7. github/gitlab credential is per-user (PAT), no longer per-project (OAuth). The previous version resolved the token via project_git_connections (per-project OAuth connection, used by the legacy createRepository). The new contract (createRepo etc.) expects a PAT (token: in Gitbeaker's constructor — PRIVATE-TOKEN), not an OAuth token (oauthToken: — Authorization: Bearer); the two aren't interchangeable (docs/adr/0004). Resolved: the credential now comes from UserCredentialRepository (a PAT registered by the user, see docs/adr/0004), decrypted directly (a raw string, without the OAuth flow's {accessToken,refreshToken} JSON wrapper). 8. The legacy GitProvider/createRepository contract retired. Confirmed by grep that ProvisionRepositoryUseCase was the only consumer of .createRepository() in all of src/ — GitProviderRegistry now returns GitProviderContract directly. This closes the "explicit debt" recorded in docs/adr/0001.

No status column on projects — provisioning|provisioned| provision_failed is derived purely from repo_bootstraps (repo-bootstrap-status.ts, the same framework-free philosophy as action-state-machine.ts), avoiding two sources of truth. repo_bootstraps doesn't use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE — concurrent provisioning for the SAME project isn't serialized in this session (the same implicit simplification the old findByProjectId guard already made). If this becomes a real problem, the future decision is about an optimistic/pessimistic lock on the row, not about redesigning the cursor. Real risk, not implemented in this session: GithubProvider.protectBranch hardcodes enforce_admins: true, which would block the commits on main if the order were reversed (protecting before committing) — that's not the case here (commits come first), but a real GitHub with main already protected outside the bootstrap could reject an administrative push later. Out of scope for this session (acceptance criteria tested against LocalGitProvider, which has no concept of protection). apps/api/scripts/demo-repo-bootstrap.ts demonstrates the end-to-end acceptance criteria: provisions with LocalGitProvider, injects a failure on the 2nd createBranch call (an observable equivalent to killing the process at step 4 of 6), runs again, converges, and prints the full event log showing the bootstrap.step_skipped events for steps 1-3 on resume.

Phase 3a assembles the agent harness in apps/engine (Elixir/OTP) BEFORE any product agent. CLAUDE.md lists 5 behaviours; this first session is explicitly LLM-free — just deterministic context assembly — and implements 3 of them: PromptAssembler, InstructionFiles, and Hooks. ToolLoop and ContextManager (which touch the LLM via the api) are left for future sessions. The engine had nothing prompt/agent/instruction-related: no table, no workspace file reader, no tokenizer, no hooks structure. This ADR records the shape decisions for that foundation.

The prompt is assembled in 5 ORDERED layers (identity → instruction_files → project_context → business_rules → task_state), each with a token budget. PromptAssembler is a PURE function agnostic to the data source (the ContextBuilder is what collects it) — this keeps the algorithm, the heart of the acceptance criteria, testable in isolation. Each layer declares a trimming strategy, applied when the budget is exceeded — always DETERMINISTIC and documented: :drop_whole_units (unit-based layers, e.g. business rules) — discards WHOLE units from the head of the list until it fits. Never truncates in the middle of a unit. The list arrives in discard order: business rules, oldest first; instruction files, lowest precedence first. A single unit larger than the budget is discarded whole (the layer can end up empty), never split. :truncate_tail (blob, e.g. project context) — keeps a prefix sized to the budget (respecting UTF-8) + a [… truncated …] marker. :keep_or_drop (blob, e.g. identity) — all-or-nothing: if it fits, keep it; if not, drop the whole layer (half an identity is useless). Rejected: truncating any layer by raw character count (it would lose the "never split a business rule" guarantee). Also rejected: a single global trimming mode — layers have different natures (list vs. blob vs. identity) and deserve different strategies, all explicit.

With no LLM and no new lib (respecting "don't install libs without justification"): the count is a local ESTIMATE via bytes/4 with a cap — the same heuristic already used in Engine.Actions.TerminalExecutor (@bytes_per_token 4). Every result is marked estimated: true in the layers and in the report. Engine.Harness.Tokenizer is a swappable behaviour via Application.get_env(:engine, :tokenizer, ...Approximate) — a real tokenizer can be plugged in later without touching the assembler.

Sources: the project workspace root's AGENTS.md + each subdirectory's AGENTS.md (recursive walk, skipping .git) + the agent's file in the database (agent_instructions). Documented precedence: database > directory > root — and, among directories, the deepest (most specific) wins over the root.
